metaDescription: Six 24V DC air conditioners for vans, skoolies and truck cabs compared on BTU, heater type, mini-split vs rooftop design and battery draw at 24 volts.
expertTake: The Outequip 24V 11,000 BTU unit is the best overall pick because it combines a 4,500 BTU PTC heater, app and remote control and a build aimed squarely at 24 volt vans and semi cabs. The UAHKPA 13,000 BTU split is the pick for owners who want maximum cooling and can accept a split layout. Anyone on a 12V system should skip this category, because a 24V unit needs a 24V bank or a converter that wastes the efficiency advantage. Prices move, so treat tiers as relative.
introParagraphs: A higher-voltage DC air conditioner suits a specific kind of rig: a semi truck cab, a bus conversion, a skoolie or a van built around a high-voltage battery bank. The higher voltage matters because the same power flows at half the current of a standard system, which means thinner cable and less voltage drop.

The category mixes rooftop units and split systems, and it mixes heat pump, PTC and cooling-only designs. The right choice depends mostly on your vehicle layout and how much capacity your battery bank can supply.

products.name: Outequip 24V 11,000 BTU rooftop AC with 4,500 BTU PTC heater
products.description:
Outequip builds this unit explicitly for 24 volt mobile electrical systems, with 11,000 BTU of cooling, a 4,500 BTU PTC heater and control by app, remote or touch panel. Running at 24 volts means the unit draws about half the amps of a comparable 12V machine, so a given cable carries more power with less loss. The listing positions it for van conversions and semi cabs, which are the rigs most likely to have a 24V bank.

The PTC heater is resistance heat, so it is simple and works in any temperature but draws power quickly. The app and touch panel are handy for tuning airflow to save battery. It sits in the highest price tier of the group, which is the cost of the fuller feature list. Compared with the 8,900 BTU unit, it offers more cooling; compared with the UAHKPA split, it is a rooftop install that does not need an indoor head unit.

Ownership is routine for a DC rooftop unit. Check the DC lugs for heat each season, keep the filter clean and verify the low-voltage cutoff matches your battery chemistry. Because the heater can pull a large share of your bank, use it for taking the chill off rather than overnight heating.
products.bestFor: 24V vans and semi cabs that want cooling, heat and app control in one rooftop unit.

products.name: 24V 8,900 BTU DC rooftop AC with equal 8,900 BTU heating
products.description:
This rooftop unit matches its heating to its cooling at 8,900 BTU each, which avoids the usual compromise where heat is a weak afterthought. It offers five operating modes including a sleep mode, and the listing claims a minimum consumption of about 0.24 kWh per hour and noise as low as 30 decibels. At 24 volts, 0.24 kWh is about 10 amps, which is gentle on a bank.

Those figures are best-case. A 30 dB claim is extremely low for a rooftop unit and should be read as the sleep-mode floor. The cooling capacity is the smallest of the rooftop units here, so it suits a small camper or van with good insulation. It sits in the lower-middle price tier. Compared with the Outequip, it trades capacity for balanced heat; compared with the SleYuYir, it heats far more.

Ownership centers on the low-voltage cutoff and cable checks. Keep the filter clean, inspect the gasket each spring and try heat mode in the shoulder season before relying on it. The five modes let you trade comfort for runtime.
products.bestFor: Small 24V campers that need equal heat and cool in a quiet unit.
pros: Sleep mode with low minimum draw

products.name: 24V 10,200 BTU non-ducted rooftop AC with scroll inverter
products.description:
This 10,200 BTU 24V unit uses a scroll inverter compressor in a high-strength ABS shell. A scroll compressor has fewer moving parts than a reciprocating design and typically runs smoothly, and the inverter lets it slow down once the cabin is cool. The 2-in-1 label means it handles both cooling and heating.

The listing is less specific than some rivals about the heater rating and noise. It sits in the upper-middle price tier. Compared with the Outequip, it lacks the app and explicit heater rating; compared with the SleYuYir, it has slightly more cooling but a less clear spec sheet.

Ownership is routine. Verify the cutoff, keep the filter clean and check the gasket annually. Ask the seller for the nameplate current at 24 volts before sizing cable, since the listing does not give it. A smooth scroll compressor can also be easier on the roof mounting.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want a smooth scroll compressor in a mid-size unit.

products.name: SleYuYir 24V 10,000 BTU rooftop AC with 3,500 BTU heat
products.description:
SleYuYir offers 10,000 BTU of cooling, 3,500 BTU of heating and a sleek low-profile ABS shell described as scratch and impact resistant. Low profile helps with clearance and wind drag. The 24V design aims to avoid the electrical headaches of converting from 12 volts.

The 3,500 BTU heater is on the small side, so think of it as a chill remover. It sits in the middle price tier. Compared with the Outequip, it offers less heat and no stated app control; compared with the 8,900 BTU unit, it cools more but heats less.

Ownership requires the usual DC checks: lugs, cutoff voltage, filter and gasket. Confirm the roof cut-out dimensions before ordering. Wind noise at highway speed is lower on a low-profile shell.
products.bestFor: Low-clearance 24V vehicles that want a compact shell.

products.name: UAHKPA 24V 13,000 BTU split-type RV air conditioner
products.description:
The UAHKPA is a split system with an indoor head and an outdoor condenser, rated 13,000 BTU, 24 volts and 900 watts running. The listing publishes unusually useful numbers: R134a refrigerant at 600 grams and a starting current of 45 amps. At 24 volts, 900 watts is about 37.5 amps running, so the starting figure shows the surge you must plan cable and fuse for.

Split systems separate noisy parts from the cabin, but they need refrigerant lines between the units and a more complex install. It sits in the lowest price tier of the group, which makes it attractive for capacity per cost. Compared with rooftop units, there is no heater listed, so it is cooling only.

Ownership requires attention to line sets, mounts and drain. The thickened hard shell resists deformation. Hire a technician for any refrigerant work. Keep the line set short and protected from road debris.
products.bestFor: Trucks and buses where a split layout fits and capacity per cost matters.

products.name: Treeligo 24V 12,000 BTU mini-split RV AC, 350 CFM
products.description:
Treeligo's 24V mini split offers 12,000 BTU, 350 CFM of airflow and a 45 dB claim with an LCD remote and panel. A mini split puts the evaporator indoors and the compressor outdoors, which keeps compressor noise away from the bed. It runs directly from a vehicle battery system.

Split installs are more work than a drop-in roof unit, and the 45 dB figure is a maker claim. It sits in the lower tier. Compared with the UAHKPA, it publishes fewer electrical details; compared with the rooftop units, it needs interior wall space.

Ownership is similar to a mini split at home: clean the filter, keep the drain clear and have a technician check refrigerant if cooling fades. Mount the outdoor unit where it gets airflow and splash protection. Confirm the indoor head's mounting height before purchase.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want compressor noise outside the cabin.

buyingCriteria.explanation: At 24 volts, 900 watts is about 37.5 amps, versus 75 amps at 12 volts. Half the current means thinner cable, less voltage drop and cooler terminals. But it only helps if your bank is 24V already. Converting a 12V system costs efficiency and money. A related benefit is that 24V alternators and chargers on trucks charge the bank directly, which helps when driving. The savings are largest on long cable runs, such as a bus with batteries at the rear.

The UAHKPA lists a 45 amp starting current, a rare honest number. Fuses, breakers and cable must handle the surge, not just the running draw. Ask for the starting figure on any unit you consider. A slow-blow fuse sized for the surge prevents nuisance trips.

Rooftop units drop into a roof opening, while the UAHKPA and Treeligo splits put the compressor outside and the head inside. Splits are quieter indoors but need refrigerant lines and a pro install. Choose based on available roof space. Split lines also need a vacuum pump and gauges, which most owners do not own. On a moving vehicle, vibration also loosens split-line fittings over time.

Outequip lists a 4,500 BTU PTC heater, the 8,900 BTU unit matches heating to cooling, and SleYuYir has 3,500 BTU. PTC heat is simple but power hungry. Pick the heating capacity you will actually use. Heat pump efficiency is not offered in this lineup, so every heater here is resistance style.

A 24V 200Ah bank holds about 4.8 kWh. At roughly 0.24 to 0.9 kWh per hour, that is anywhere from five to twenty hours depending on the unit and load. Size the bank to the real draw, not the best-case minimum. Solar and alternator charging should be able to replace at least half of a day's use.

Without a cutoff a DC air conditioner can drain a bank to damaging levels. Set it to match your battery chemistry. This is the cheapest insurance in the build. Look for a setting you can change without opening the unit. Lithium packs have their own BMS cutoff, but a separate one at the unit is still sensible.

specDecoder.meaning: Power in steady operation; divide by 24 for amps. That helps size cable and fuses.
Surge when the compressor starts. Always size the fuse for it.

howWeEvaluated.title: Electrical fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We converted watts to amps at 24 volts and weighed start-up surge. The UAHKPA's published 45 A start was the clearest data. We assumed a 24V system as the baseline.

howWeEvaluated.title: Heating
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared 3,500, 4,500 and 8,900 BTU heating ratings. Resistance heat was scored for reliability, not efficiency.

howWeEvaluated.title: Layout
howWeEvaluated.description: We separated rooftop from split designs. Install difficulty counted, since splits need a pro. A rooftop unit can be a weekend job, while a split can take several days.

howWeEvaluated.title: Noise claims
howWeEvaluated.description: We treated 30 to 45 dB claims as best case. Real noise is higher than a sleep-mode figure.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value
howWeEvaluated.description: We judged tiers from the UAHKPA at the low end to the Outequip at the top. Value here also includes how much installation work you must pay for.

howToChoose.intro: Vehicle type decides layout before it decides brand. A semi cab and a skoolie have very different roof space and wall space.
Tiers are relative, and the spread is wide. The extra spend mostly buys heater capacity and control features.

cards.label: Rooftop
cards.text: Outequip, SleYuYir and the scroll unit drop into a roof opening.

cards.label: Split
cards.text: UAHKPA and Treeligo keep the compressor outside but need refrigerant lines.

howToChoose.note: No roof space, choose split; simple install, choose rooftop. Rooftop installs also reuse the same roof opening if you ever swap the unit.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Low minimum draw, a sleep mode and a reliable cutoff. A thin insulation layer on the roof and windows often saves more battery than a bigger unit.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The 8,900 BTU unit lists 0.24 kWh minimum and a sleep mode. Use sleep mode overnight to reduce the draw.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You want app control and strong heat, pointing to the Outequip. Remember that a heater and compressor together can pull most of a small bank, so stagger their use.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You only need cooling, pointing to the UAHKPA. Add a shunt monitor either way, so you know the real amps.

maintenance.why: Airflow loss reduces cooling and can ice the coil. Wash the foam and dry it fully before refitting.
High current heats loose lugs. Look for discolored insulation.
Leaks and vibration cause damage on a moving vehicle.
Protects the battery bank. Confirm it matches your chemistry. Test it by watching the voltage drop under load.
Dirty coils raise power use and head pressure. Use a soft brush and low-pressure water.

faq.a: Yes. Converting from 12V wastes the advantage and adds a failure point. A DC-DC converter exists but is not ideal for an air conditioner load.
A 200Ah 24V bank holds about 4.8 kWh, so hours depend on the unit's draw and the weather. Solar and alternator charging extend it.
Tiers run from UAHKPA at the low end to Outequip at the top. Prices change, so check listings. The spread is wide, so decide on layout first.
Rooftop is simpler to install, split is quieter indoors. Check for roof space first.
No, but it works in any temperature and is simple. Use it sparingly on battery.
